source: Nieuwenstein, Wierenga, Morey, Wicherts, Blom, Wagenmakers, van Rijn (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage
finding: A large replication of the unconscious thought advantage (UTA: distraction beats deliberation for complex choices), built to meet the proponents' own optimal conditions, found no effect.
numbers: N=399. Correct choice: deliberation 55.61% (n=196) vs distraction 55.17% (n=203) in the first-done condition. Bayes factor favours the null by 7.83.
limits: One paradigm (multi-attribute choice), not insight or divergent tasks. Immediate-incubation design, so it does not test delayed incubation.
agent_relevance: Do not build a 'let it sit, then choose' step on the claim that unconscious weighing improves decisions. Evidence for that is weak.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) meta-analysis part
finding: Across 61 UTA studies the pooled effect is small and shrinks to zero after correcting for publication bias. Significant UTA results sit in low-precision (small-N) studies.
numbers: 61 studies, N 40 to 399, g range -0.74 to 1.48. Random effects g=0.15, CI [0.03,0.26], p=0.01. Only 16 significant effects (12 UTA, 4 favouring deliberation); 45 non-significant. Funnel asymmetry Z=2.11, p=.04. Trim-and-fill (10 imputed): g=0.018, CI [-0.10,0.14], p=0.77.
limits: Choice tasks only. Small-study effects can also come from heterogeneity, but the replication points the same way.
agent_relevance: Treat any incubation or 'sleep on it' gain from small studies as suspect. Check for a precision-effect link before trusting.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) test of the moderator account
finding: Two rival accounts were tested. Reliability account: UTA is noise from an unreliable paradigm. Moderator account: UTA appears only under special conditions (Strick et al. 2011). The big study met all the listed moderators and still found nothing, favouring the reliability account. A claimed gender-specific UTA also failed.
numbers: Replication followed Strick et al. (2011) recommendations. Males: deliberation 50.8% (n=130) vs distraction 55.4% (n=130). Females n=269 deliberation 61.7%. Strick meta-analysis effect cited as d=.218.
limits: The authors admit the prior for H1 may understate what proponents would predict.
agent_relevance: When a claimed effect needs many moderators to appear, expect it to fail in generic use.

source: Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014) Creativity - the unconscious foundations of the incubation period
finding: Review by proponents of unconscious thought. Lists the evidence base for incubation and the null results. Concludes incubation likely mixes conscious and unconscious phases.
numbers: Reports Dodds et al. (2003): 29 of 39 experiments found a significant incubation effect. Sio & Ormerod (2009): 117 studies, positive overall effect. Read first 100,000 of about 133,700 characters.
limits: Authors favour unconscious thought. Few standardized effect sizes given. Last third of the page not read.
agent_relevance: Incubation is real on average but small and task dependent. Do not treat it as a dependable operator.

source: Olton & Johnson (1976); Ritter et al. (2012b); Zhong et al. (2008); Ashby et al. (2011); Pachur & Forrer (2013) as listed in Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014)
finding: Review lists null or contested results: Olton & Johnson found no incubation effect. Zhong 2008: incubation raised accessibility of answers but not correct reports. Ritter 2012b: idea generation was equal after conscious and unconscious thought; only selection improved. Ashby 2011 and Pachur & Forrer 2013 did not support unconscious weighting.
numbers: No effect sizes given in the review for these items.
limits: Originals not opened. Taken from the review page.
agent_relevance: Gains from incubation may come from selection or accessibility, not new idea generation. Generate first, select after a gap.

source: Yang et al. (2012) break length; Barrett (1993), Wagner et al. (2004), Walker et al. (2002), Cai et al. (2009), Sio et al. (2012) as reported in Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014)
finding: Sleep and break-length studies. Break length shows an inverted U: 3 minutes beat 1 and 5 minutes. Sleep helped hidden-rule discovery and harder remote-associate items but not easier ones.
numbers: Yang: 3 min beat 1 and 5 min. Wagner: about 60% of sleepers found the hidden rule vs 23% awake. Walker: REM awakening gave 32% anagram advantage over NREM. Cai: REM naps about 40% better on remote associates. Barrett: 25% dreamed an answer.
limits: Originals not opened; figures as quoted in the review.
agent_relevance: Optimal pause is task dependent and easy items gain nothing. Do not add a fixed delay everywhere.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving
finding: Hypothesis paper. Argues three accounts compete: unconscious work, intermittent conscious work, beneficial forgetting. His own divergent-thinking studies favoured unconscious work. States that the basic existence of delayed incubation effects is established, especially for divergent problems.
numbers: Cites Sio & Ormerod (2009): 117 studies, mean d=0.29 (low to medium) across insight and divergent tasks. Cites Strick et al. (2011): 92 decision studies, g=0.224 for immediate incubation.
limits: Author's own lab supports one side. The paper notes intermittent-conscious-work checks were seldom run in the literature.
agent_relevance: Plan for small gains (d about 0.3) at best, and not on every task type.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (via Gilhooly 2016)
finding: Key moderator: benefits are larger when the break is filled with an undemanding task than with a demanding task or no task. Effect reported for insight and divergent tasks.
numbers: 117 studies, mean d=0.29. Direct page returned only a loading shell, so figures come from Gilhooly 2016.
limits: Original not opened. Other moderators not verified.
agent_relevance: If an agent pause exists, make it low-demand (cheap side work), not a blank wait and not a hard second task.

source: Strick et al. (2011) unconscious thought meta-analysis (via Gilhooly 2016)
finding: Proponent meta-analysis of 92 decision studies found a small benefit. Moderators: more options, shorter presentation, shorter incubation, and a configural mindset gave larger effects. Later large-scale work (b01-b03) did not hold up.
numbers: g=0.224, 92 studies.
limits: Original not opened. Pre-dates the bias-corrected re-analysis.
agent_relevance: The moderators were fitted post hoc, which is why the later replication may have failed.

source: Gilhooly et al. (2012, 2013, 2015) divergent-thinking incubation studies (via Gilhooly 2016)
finding: Immediate versus delayed incubation on the Alternative Uses task. Resource-competing interpolated tasks reduced the benefit, which the author reads as support for unconscious work over intermittent conscious work. Ritter review adds that cross-domain filler worked better than same-domain filler.
numbers: No numbers in the pages read.
limits: Originals not opened. Interpretation is the author's and is contested (see b11).
agent_relevance: Choose filler work that does not use the same resource as the task (different modality).

source: Commentary (2017) on Gilhooly: Incubation and Intuition in Creative Problem Solving
finding: Dual-process rival to unconscious work. For insight (convergent) problems, overcoming an impasse needs controlled processes (working memory, inhibition, switching), so incubation cannot be only unconscious. Unconscious work may fit divergent tasks.
numbers: No new data. Cites Zhong et al. (2008) as an insightful-incubation result that unconscious work alone cannot explain.
limits: Commentary, no experiment. Conscious-control claim is indirect.
agent_relevance: Divergent and insight tasks may need different operators. Pauses for divergent search, active restructuring for impasse.

source: Du, Gordon, Tolmie (2025) The role of mind wandering during incubation in divergent and convergent creative thinking
finding: Mind wandering during a 0-back break had no effect on divergent thinking, failing to replicate Baird et al. (2012) on that outcome. For convergent items, wandering with awareness helped easy repeated items; wandering without awareness hurt moderate-difficulty novel items. Divergent and convergent scores were not correlated.
numbers: N=85. 0-back accuracy 0.96 here vs 0.87 in Baird; Steindorf et al. ~0.93 and Murray et al. ~0.91 also found null effects. Incubation raised UUT fluency, mostly on repeated items.
limits: Small sample. High 0-back accuracy may have left no capacity for wandering. Verbal filler may compete with verbal task.
agent_relevance: Gains showed up on repeated problems, so part of the gain is a second try, not incubation. Compare any pause with a plain retry.

source: Baird et al. (2012) Inspired by distraction (via Ritter & Dijksterhuis 2014 and Du et al. 2025)
finding: Undemanding task during break improved creative solutions more than demanding task, rest, or no break, and only on repeated problems. Later attempts (Steindorf, Murray, Du 2025) did not replicate the divergent effect.
numbers: No numbers in the pages read.
limits: Original not opened. Effect confined to repeated items.
agent_relevance: Repeated-problem effect equals a practice benefit. Test an agent pause against a plain second attempt.

source: Mind wandering simultaneously prolongs reactions and promotes creative incubation (2017) Sci Rep
finding: People who mind-wandered more during an attention task (SART) solved more compound remote associate items afterwards. No such link existed in the pre-task baseline, ruling out a simple trait explanation. Mind wandering also cost attention: slower and more variable responses.
numbers: Experiment 1, N=28: Kendall tau=0.28, p=0.03 (post), tau=0.12, p=0.36 (pre). Reaction time off-task 448 vs on-task 439 ms, p=0.01, r=0.32. RT SD 29 vs 17 ms, p=0.001. Off-task rates 34%, 47%, 48% across three experiments.
limits: Correlational and small (N=28 in the reported test). Mind wandering was self-reported by probes.
agent_relevance: Benefit is tied to a pre-set problem plus a drifting period. A pure idle gap is not shown to do the same.

source: Mind wandering during creative incubation predicts increases in creative performance in a writing task (2025) Sci Rep, preregistered
finding: Preregistered test of four 10-minute break types (0-back, 2-back, mindfulness, no break). No difference in creative improvement across break types. Within people, more self-reported mind wandering predicted more improvement, but only when the same prompt was reused, not for a new prompt. GPT-4 ratings agreed with the semantic-distance score.
numbers: N=200 participants. Only the abstract and design were read; coefficients not extracted.
limits: Correlation inside conditions, not randomised. Same-prompt only, so problem-specific.
agent_relevance: Break type did not matter. This cuts against designing a particular 'wander' filler for the agent.

source: Chandolia, Kidd, Paladino, Smith (2026) Comparing aha moments in problem solving and generative ideation
finding: Cites a Smith lab finding that alternating between category types during generation gave an incubation effect for ad hoc and sense-impression categories only. The authors say their own study did not manipulate restructuring, incubation or forgetting fixation.
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Only incubation-related sentences were read; full paper not read.
agent_relevance: Incubation-like alternation helps flexible categories, not rigid ones.

source: Vul & Pashler (2007) Incubation benefits only after people have been misdirected (title seen in Europe PMC; not opened)
finding: Title states the boundary condition: incubation helps only after misleading cues. This matches the forgetting-fixation account of Smith & Blankenship (1991). The 2026 REM study (b18) cites the same idea.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the title and bibliographic record were seen.
agent_relevance: Use a pause only after the agent is stuck on a wrong frame, not before it has tried.

source: REM sleep favors restructuring of problem-related semantic associations (2026) Sci Rep
finding: 90-minute incubation with wake, NREM or REM sleep after a failed riddle attempt. REM reshaped the semantic network, combining remote concepts and weakening strong but solution-irrelevant links. This did not raise solving success. Authors read it as consistent with forgetting fixation.
numbers: N=111 first attempt; 25 solved (22.5%). After break 10 of 84 non-solvers solved (11.9%). Wake 20% (4/20), NREM 5% (1/20), REM 11.4% (5/44), Fisher p=0.36. Network analysis groups: Wake n=17, NREM 17, REM 31.
limits: Low solving rate gave little power. Sleep group n=83 vs wake 28.
agent_relevance: Restructuring and solving are separate. A quiet period can reshape memory without producing the answer.

source: Sleep facilitates problem solving with no additional gain through targeted memory reactivation (2021) Front Behav Neurosci
finding: Experiment 1: a night of sleep beat daytime wake on an unsolved video-game problem. Experiment 2: cueing the problem during sleep added nothing. An earlier TMR gain was not reproduced.
numbers: Exp 1: 62% of sleepers solved vs 24% of wake group, over about 10 hours. Exp 2: 56% (SWS cue) and 58% (REM cue) vs 57% wake-cue. More slow-wave sleep gave better odds.
limits: Sleep, not mere time. Cueing effect not replicated.
agent_relevance: Offline consolidation helps, but extra cue replay does not.

source: A critical review and meta-analysis of the unconscious thought effect in medical decision making (2015) Front Psychol
finding: Distraction did not help clinician decisions. Expertise moderated in the opposite direction to the theory: unconscious thought seemed to hurt experts and perhaps help novices. Bayes factors mostly supported the null.
numbers: 17 contrasts; z=0.35, p=0.73; I2=69.9%, Q(16)=51.83. Experts d=-0.14, CI [-0.32,0.04]; novices d=0.24, CI [-0.02,0.51]; expertise Q(1)=5.71, p=0.017. Distractor type Q(1)=3.83, p=0.050, driven by one word-search study.
limits: Medical vignettes only. Heterogeneity high.
agent_relevance: Expertise was not a boost for pausing. Do not assume strong agents gain from incubation.

source: Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (2020) Mem Cogn
finding: Cheap necklace problem. A 2-week gap helped more when people worked with physical chains than with pen and paper. When the format changed across the gap, only a high-interactivity second try improved.
numbers: Time 1: 43% solved with chains (12) vs 6% (2) with pen and paper, chi2(1,N=63)=12. Time 2 among Time-1 failures: 44% (7 of 16) high interactivity vs 15% (5 of 33) low, chi2(1,N=49)=4. Everyone who solved at Time 1 solved again.
limits: Second attempt is a repeated test. Two-week gap is far beyond a normal break.
agent_relevance: Action in the environment (tools, execution) at the retry mattered. Pair any pause with a tool-using retry.

source: Orru, Piarulli, Conversano, Gemignani (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in LLMs using ChatGPT, Front AI
finding: ChatGPT answered 30 verbal insight problems (15 practice, 15 transfer) and matched the most probable score for 20 human subjects. Its answer pattern was within the top 5% of probable human outcomes. No incubation step was tested.
numbers: 30 problems, human norms from 20 subjects. Solution counts per set not extracted here.
limits: Old model (2023). No pause manipulation. Small human norm sample. Contamination risk with published problems.
agent_relevance: LLMs solve many insight riddles in one pass, so there may be no impasse to incubate through.

source: Huang, Liu, Yang (2026) Evaluation of LLMs as tools, models, and partners in creative thinking research, selective review
finding: Review covering Jan 2018 to Jun 2026. LLMs exceed average humans on divergent thinking in most independent comparisons. The capability axis concludes models replicate associative effects but fail to capture insight, incubation, evaluation and individual differences.
numbers: Hedges g about 0.5 to 2.6 over average humans on divergent tasks. Automated scoring ICC at least 0.80, r at least 0.70 in selected studies.
limits: Narrative review. Incubation is mentioned only in passing and no LLM incubation experiment is listed in the text read.
agent_relevance: No direct test of LLM incubation was found here. Do not claim the agent gains from a pause without own measurement.

source: Lin, Snell, Wang, Packer, Wooders, Stoica, Gonzalez (2025) Sleep-time compute: beyond inference scaling at test time
finding: Closest machine analogue to incubation: the model reasons offline about a context before any question arrives. This cuts test-time compute and raises accuracy when questions are predictable.
numbers: Same accuracy with about 5x less test-time compute. Up to +13% on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and +18% on Stateful AIME. 2.5x lower cost per query on Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic.
limits: Abstract page only. It is pre-computation, not forgetting or insight. Gains depend on predictable queries.
agent_relevance: Pre-thinking helps when the future question is predictable. It is not evidence for creative incubation.

source: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC generation waiting period (2026) Front Psychol
finding: Design students' behaviour while waiting for AI images. Creativity depended on whether the waiting task stayed on the creative task. The condition labelled GP scored lowest. Task relevance and workload interacted.
numbers: Experiment 3 N=60 (2x2). Four-condition ANOVA F(3,56)=9.201, p<0.001, eta2p=0.330; GP lower than RS, DB and RB, all p<0.001. Task relevance F(1,56)=10.864, p=0.002; workload F(1,56)=9.612, p=0.003; interaction F(1,56)=7.126, p=0.010.
limits: Condition codes (GP, RS, DB, RB) not decoded in the pages read. Students, not agents. Incubation reading is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Staying task-relevant during a wait did not hurt and may beat disengaging, which contradicts the usual unrelated-filler advice.
